questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: The integrated rate law for a zero-order reaction A → products is:
options: ln[A] = ln[A]<sub>0</sub> − kt
[A] = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt
[A] = [A]<sub>0</sub>e<sup>−kt</sup>
questions.explanation: For a zero-order reaction, rate = k (independent of concentration), so integrating −d[A]/dt = k directly (no logarithms needed) gives the straight-line relation [A] = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt.
questions.hint: Zero order is the only one of the common orders whose integrated law is a plain straight line in [A] itself, with no logarithms.
distractor_logic: States the form used for a second-order reaction, not zero order.
States the logarithmic (first-order) form of the integrated rate law rather than the direct linear zero-order form.
States the first-order integrated rate law's exponential form instead of the zero-order linear form.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: For a zero-order reaction, the units of the rate constant k are:
options: s<sup>−1</sup>
mol<sup>−1</sup> L s<sup>−1</sup>
mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
mol<sup>−2</sup> L<sup>2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: General units of k are mol<sup>1−n</sup> L<sup>n−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> for order n. For n = 0: mol<sup>1</sup> L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> = mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> — the same units as rate itself, since for zero order, rate = k exactly.
questions.hint: For zero order, k has the SAME units as rate itself: mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>.
distractor_logic: Gives the units appropriate for a first-order reaction instead of zero order.
Gives the units appropriate for a second-order reaction instead of zero order.
Gives the units appropriate for a third-order reaction instead of zero order.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: For a zero-order reaction, a plot of [A] (concentration of reactant) on the y-axis against time t on the x-axis gives:
options: an exponentially decaying curve, with the y-intercept equal to [A]<sub>0</sub>
a straight line with a negative slope equal to −k, and a y-intercept equal to [A]<sub>0</sub>
a straight line with a positive slope equal to k, and a y-intercept of zero
a straight line with slope k and y-intercept equal to 1/[A]<sub>0</sub>
questions.explanation: Rearranging [A] = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt into the form y = mx + c: y = [A], x = t, slope m = −k, intercept c = [A]<sub>0</sub>. This straight-line behaviour (negative slope, [A]<sub>0</sub> intercept) is the graphical signature of a zero-order reaction.
questions.hint: Compare [A] = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt directly to the equation of a straight line, y = mx + c.
distractor_logic: Describes the shape of a first-order concentration-time plot (exponential decay), not the straight line characteristic of zero order.
Gets the wrong sign for the slope (concentration falls over time, so the slope must be negative, not positive) and the wrong intercept (should be [A]₀, not zero).
Confuses this plot with the (1/[A] vs t) plot used for second-order reactions; for zero order it is [A] itself, not 1/[A], that is linear in time.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: The half-life of a zero-order reaction is given by t<sub>1/2</sub> =
options: [A]<sub>0</sub> / 2k
1/(k[A]<sub>0</sub>)
2k/[A]<sub>0</sub>
questions.explanation: Setting [A] = [A]<sub>0</sub>/2 in [A] = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt: [A]<sub>0</sub>/2 = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt<sub>1/2</sub>, so kt<sub>1/2</sub> = [A]<sub>0</sub>/2, giving t<sub>1/2</sub> = [A]<sub>0</sub>/2k. Notice this DOES depend on the initial concentration, unlike the first-order half-life.
questions.hint: Unlike first-order half-life, the zero-order half-life formula explicitly contains [A]<sub>0</sub>.
distractor_logic: States the half-life formula for a first-order reaction, not zero order.
States a form resembling the second-order half-life formula, not zero order.
Inverts the correct zero-order half-life expression.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A zero-order reaction has [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.50 mol L<sup>−1</sup> and rate constant k = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. What is [A] after 100 s?
options: 0.20 mol L<sup>−1</sup>
0.10 mol L<sup>−1</sup>
0.30 mol L<sup>−1</sup>
0.48 mol L<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: [A] = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt = 0.50 − (2.0×10<sup>−3</sup>)(100) = 0.50 − 0.20 = 0.30 mol L<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: First compute kt (the amount consumed), then subtract that from the initial concentration.
distractor_logic: Reports only the amount consumed (kt = 0.20) as if it were the remaining concentration, instead of subtracting it from [A]₀.
Subtracts kt from [A]₀ twice over (double-counts the consumption), giving too little A remaining.
Forgets to convert k to consistent units before multiplying by t, effectively using k as if it were 2.0×10<sup>−4</sup> instead of 2.0×10<sup>−3</sup>.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: For a zero-order reaction, [A] falls from 1.00 mol L<sup>−1</sup> to 0.70 mol L<sup>−1</sup> in 150 s. What is the rate constant k?
options: 4.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
1.5 × 10<sup>−2</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
7.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: For zero order, k = ([A]<sub>0</sub> − [A])/t = (1.00 − 0.70)/150 = 0.30/150 = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Zero order uses a simple linear formula — no logarithms or the 2.303 factor are needed here.
distractor_logic: Wrongly applies the first-order logarithmic formula (dividing by 2.303 and taking a log ratio) to what is stated to be zero-order data.
Divides the wrong quantity by time — uses [A]₀/t (1.00/150) instead of the concentration change Δ[A]/t (0.30/150).
Divides by the wrong time value, as if t were 1/7th of the stated 150 s.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A zero-order reaction has [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.80 mol L<sup>−1</sup> and k = 4.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. How long does it take for A to be completely consumed?
questions.explanation: Complete consumption means [A] = 0, so from [A] = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt: 0 = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt, giving t = [A]<sub>0</sub>/k = 0.80/(4.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 200 s.
questions.hint: Set [A] = 0 in the integrated rate law and solve for t — this time is TWICE the half-life for zero order.
distractor_logic: Halves the correct time, perhaps by using [A]₀/(2k) (the zero-order half-life formula) instead of the time for complete consumption, [A]₀/k.
Multiplies [A]₀ and k together instead of dividing [A]₀ by k.
Divides [A]₀ by k but drops a factor of 10 somewhere in the arithmetic, giving too short a time.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A zero-order reaction has [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.60 mol L<sup>−1</sup> and k = 1.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. What is its half-life?
questions.explanation: t<sub>1/2</sub> = [A]<sub>0</sub>/2k = 0.60/(2 × 1.5×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 0.60/(3.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 200 s.
questions.hint: Don't forget the factor of 2 in the denominator: t<sub>1/2</sub> = [A]<sub>0</sub>/(2k), not [A]<sub>0</sub>/k.
distractor_logic: Multiplies instead of dividing by 2k, or misplaces a decimal point while computing 0.60/(2×1.5×10<sup>−3</sup>).
Uses the first-order half-life formula (0.693/k) with the given k value, rather than the zero-order formula that requires [A]₀.
Forgets to divide by k at all, or applies an extra unwarranted factor of 2, doubling the correct half-life.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: The catalytic surface decomposition of a gas gives the following data: at t = 0 s, [A] = 0.500 mol L<sup>−1</sup>; at t = 100 s, [A] = 0.400 mol L<sup>−1</sup>; at t = 200 s, [A] = 0.300 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. Confirm the reaction is zero order, find k, and predict [A] at t = 350 s.
options: k = 1.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; [A] at 350 s = 0 mol L<sup>−1</sup> (reaction has already finished)
k = 1.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; [A] at 350 s = 0.250 mol L<sup>−1</sup>
k = 5.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; [A] at 350 s = 0.325 mol L<sup>−1</sup>
k = 1.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (constant across both intervals, confirming zero order); [A] at 350 s = 0.150 mol L<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: Interval 1: k = (0.500−0.400)/100 = 1.0×10<sup>−3</sup>. Interval 2: k = (0.400−0.300)/100 = 1.0×10<sup>−3</sup>. Since k is the same in both intervals, [A] vs t is linear, confirming zero order. Using [A] = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt: [A] at 350 s = 0.500 − (1.0×10<sup>−3</sup>)(350) = 0.500 − 0.350 = 0.150 mol L<sup>−1</sup>.

distractor_logic: Correctly finds k but wrongly assumes the reaction must be finished (all A consumed) well before t=350s, when in fact [A]₀/k = 500 s, so the reaction is still ongoing at 350 s.

Uses only one of the two intervals inconsistently, averaging in a spurious extra factor and landing on half the correct k, then propagates that error forward.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: Ammonia decomposes on a hot platinum surface as a zero-order reaction (the surface is fully saturated with NH<sub>3</sub>). Given [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.400 mol L<sup>−1</sup> and k = 8.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, what percentage of NH<sub>3</sub> has decomposed after 250 s?
questions.explanation: Amount reacted = kt = (8.0×10<sup>−4</sup>)(250) = 0.20 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. % decomposed = (0.20/0.400) × 100 = 50%.
questions.hint: First find the absolute amount reacted (kt), then express it as a percentage of the original concentration.
distractor_logic: Computes the amount reacted correctly but then divides it by double the initial concentration instead of the actual initial concentration.
Uses the wrong reference concentration when computing the percentage, effectively dividing by 0.32 instead of 0.400.
Confuses percentage decomposed with percentage remaining, or miscalculates kt as 0.32 instead of 0.20 through a units slip.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: Two identical zero-order reactions are run with the same rate constant k, but reaction P starts with [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.40 mol L<sup>−1</sup> while reaction Q starts with double that concentration, [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.80 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. How does the half-life of Q compare to that of P?
options: Q's half-life is exactly double P's half-life
Q and P have identical half-lives
Q's half-life is exactly half of P's half-life
Q's half-life is four times P's half-life
questions.explanation: t<sub>1/2</sub> = [A]<sub>0</sub>/2k, so half-life is directly proportional to [A]<sub>0</sub>. Doubling [A]<sub>0</sub> (as in reaction Q) exactly doubles the half-life. This is the opposite of first-order behaviour, where half-life is completely independent of the initial concentration.
questions.hint: For zero order, t<sub>1/2</sub> is directly proportional to [A]<sub>0</sub> — unlike first order, where it is constant regardless of [A]<sub>0</sub>.
distractor_logic: Applies the first-order rule (half-life independent of initial concentration) to a zero-order reaction, where half-life actually depends directly and proportionally on initial concentration.
Confuses zero order with first order, where doubling initial concentration has no effect on half-life — here it wrongly assumes the opposite (inverse) relationship instead of the correct direct one.
Assumes t<sub>1/2</sub> scales with the square of [A]₀, when the zero-order half-life formula shows a simple direct (linear) proportionality, not a squared one.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A zero-order reaction has [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.900 mol L<sup>−1</sup> and k = 3.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. How long does it take for 75% of A to be consumed?
questions.explanation: 75% consumed means the amount reacted = 0.75 × [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.75 × 0.900 = 0.675 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. Since amount reacted = kt: t = 0.675/(3.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 225 s.
questions.hint: First find the absolute amount that must react (75% of the initial concentration), then divide by k to get time.
distractor_logic: Divides the correct answer by an extra unwarranted factor of about 3.33, likely from confusing the amount reacted with the amount remaining.
Uses 0.75 as a multiplier on the wrong base quantity, effectively computing 0.75 × [A]₀ and then dividing by an incorrect combined factor rather than cleanly by k.
Computes the time for 100% consumption ([A]₀/k = 300 s) instead of scaling down for the 75% completion point specifically requested.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A zero-order surface reaction has k = 5.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> and [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.600 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. Find the average rate of the reaction over the interval t = 0 to t = 60 s, and the instantaneous rate at t = 60 s. How do these two values compare, and why?
options: Both are 5.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> only by coincidence at this particular value of k; in general zero-order rates still fall with time like any other order
Average rate = 5.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, but instantaneous rate at 60 s is lower because [A] has decreased by then
Average rate cannot be computed without knowing [A] at t=60s explicitly, since rate always depends on remaining concentration

Both equal 5.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> — average and instantaneous rate are identical throughout a zero-order reaction, because the rate never changes with concentration or time (until the reactant runs out)
questions.explanation: For a zero-order reaction, rate = k at every single instant, regardless of how much A remains (as long as some A is still present). This means average rate over any interval and instantaneous rate at any point within that interval are always numerically identical — both equal k = 5.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> here, and this is a defining structural feature of zero order, not a coincidence tied to these particular numbers.
questions.hint: For zero order specifically, rate is literally always equal to k — average and instantaneous rate can never differ.
distractor_logic: Correctly gets the numeric answer but then denies the underlying reason, wrongly suggesting zero order is a special coincidence rather than a structural feature (rate = k always, for every order-zero reaction, not just this one).
Wrongly imports first-order-style reasoning (rate falling as concentration falls) into a zero-order case, where rate is by definition independent of concentration.

Assumes rate always requires knowing the current concentration, which is only true for orders greater than zero; for zero order the rate is simply the constant k, with no concentration dependence at all.

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A zero-order reaction has t<sub>1/2</sub> = 50 s when [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.20 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. If the same reaction is instead started with [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.50 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, find the new half-life, and also find how long it takes to reach the point where exactly half of the ORIGINAL 0.20 mol L⁻¹ worth of material would have reacted (i.e. 0.10 mol L⁻¹ consumed) starting from the new, higher initial concentration.
options: k = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; new half-life = 50 s (unchanged, as if this were first order); time to consume 0.10 mol L<sup>−1</sup> = 50 s
k = 4.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; new half-life = 62.5 s; time to consume 0.10 mol L<sup>−1</sup> = 25 s
k = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; new half-life = 125 s; time to consume 0.10 mol L<sup>−1</sup> from the new start = 50 s
k = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; new half-life = 125 s; time to consume 0.10 mol L<sup>−1</sup> = 125 s
questions.explanation: From the original data: t<sub>1/2</sub> = [A]<sub>0</sub>/2k ⇒ 50 = 0.20/(2k) ⇒ k = 0.20/100 = 2.0×10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. New half-life (at [A]<sub>0</sub>=0.50) = 0.50/(2×2.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 125 s. Time to consume a FIXED 0.10 mol L<sup>−1</sup> (regardless of starting concentration, since rate = k is constant): t = 0.10/(2.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 50 s — which is simply the original half-life value, since consuming a fixed absolute amount always takes the same time at a fixed k, no matter what the starting concentration was.
questions.hint: Time to consume a fixed absolute AMOUNT (not fraction) of reactant depends only on k, never on the starting concentration, for zero order.
distractor_logic: Correctly finds k but then wrongly imports the first-order rule that half-life doesn't depend on initial concentration, when for zero order it explicitly does.
Misreads the original data, computing k as 0.20/(50) directly without the factor of 2 in the half-life formula, which distorts both k and everything derived from it.

Gets k and the new half-life correct but then confuses 'time to consume a fixed absolute amount' with 'time to reach the new half-life', wrongly assuming these coincide when the fixed amount (0.10) is not actually half of the new, larger initial concentration (0.50).

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: Data for a reaction: at t = 0 s, [A] = 0.500 mol L<sup>−1</sup>; at t = 100 s, [A] = 0.400 mol L<sup>−1</sup>; at t = 200 s, [A] = 0.320 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. A student assumes this is zero order without checking, and predicts [A] at t = 300 s using k from the first interval alone. Is the zero-order assumption justified, and what does a proper check reveal?
options: No — k from interval 1 is 1.0×10<sup>−3</sup> but k from interval 2 is only 8.0×10<sup>−4</sup>, so [A] vs t is NOT linear and the reaction is not zero order; the student's prediction from interval 1 alone would be unreliable
No, because zero-order reactions must always have exactly equal time intervals in any data table, which these do (100 s each), so the order cannot be determined at all from this data
Yes, because any reaction where [A] keeps decreasing over time must be zero order by definition
Yes — both intervals give k close to 1.0×10<sup>−3</sup>, confirming zero order, so the student's approach is valid
questions.explanation: Interval 1: k = (0.500−0.400)/100 = 1.0×10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. Interval 2: k = (0.400−0.320)/100 = 8.0×10<sup>−4</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. Since these two values of k are noticeably different (the rate of concentration loss is slowing down over time, not staying constant), [A] vs t is not truly linear, and the reaction is NOT zero order over this range — a student who fit only the first interval and extrapolated linearly to t=300s would get an unreliable prediction.
questions.hint: Always compute k from at least two separate intervals of the SAME data set before trusting that a reaction is zero order — a single interval can never confirm order.
distractor_logic: Invents an irrelevant requirement about equal time intervals; equal spacing of data points has nothing to do with whether the underlying kinetics are zero order — what matters is whether the computed k stays constant.
Confuses 'concentration decreasing over time' (true for every order) with the specific zero-order signature (constant k, i.e. constant absolute rate of decrease), which is not what this data shows.
Misreads or miscalculates the second interval's k value, wrongly concluding the two intervals agree when they actually differ meaningfully (1.0×10<sup>−3</sup> vs 8.0×10<sup>−4</sup>).

questions.topic: Zero Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A zero-order reaction has rate constant k = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> at 300 K and k = 8.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> at 320 K. Calculate the activation energy E<sub>a</sub> for this reaction (use R = 8.314 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>).
options: E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 13.8 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 55.3 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 5.53 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 110.6 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: Using log(k<sub>2</sub>/k<sub>1</sub>) = (E<sub>a</sub>/2.303R)(1/T<sub>1</sub> − 1/T<sub>2</sub>): log(8.0×10<sup>−3</sup>/2.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) = log(4) = 0.602. 1/300 − 1/320 = 0.003333 − 0.003125 = 2.083×10<sup>−5</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>. So E<sub>a</sub> = (2.303 × 8.314 × 0.602)/(2.083×10<sup>−5</sup>) ≈ 55,300 J mol<sup>−1</sup> = 55.3 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. Notice E<sub>a</sub> is calculated the same way regardless of the reaction's order (zero order here) — the two-temperature Arrhenius equation only needs two k values, not concentration data.
questions.hint: The two-temperature Arrhenius formula uses only k values at two temperatures — the reaction's order is irrelevant to this particular calculation.
distractor_logic: Forgets to multiply by the factor of R (8.314) at the correct stage, or divides where it should multiply, understating E<sub>a</sub> by roughly a factor of 4.
Loses a full factor of 10 somewhere in unit handling between J mol<sup>−1</sup> and kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

questions.question: The integrated rate law for a first-order reaction A → products can be written as:
options: 1/[A] − 1/[A]<sub>0</sub> = kt
[A] = [A]<sub>0</sub> − kt
questions.explanation: Starting from −d[A]/[A] = k dt and integrating gives ln([A]<sub>0</sub>/[A]) = kt, i.e. k = (1/t)ln([A]<sub>0</sub>/[A]). Converting to log base 10 (ln x = 2.303 log<sub>10</sub>x) gives k = (2.303/t) log<sub>10</sub>([A]<sub>0</sub>/[A]).
questions.hint: The 2.303 sits on top, multiplying the log term, with t on the bottom.
distractor_logic: States the second-order integrated rate law instead of the first-order one.
Inverts the 2.303/t factor, placing t in the numerator instead of the denominator.
States the zero-order integrated rate law instead of the first-order one.

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: For a first-order reaction, the units of the rate constant k are always:
options: s<sup>−1</sup> (time inverse, with no concentration units at all)
mol<sup>−1</sup> L s<sup>−1</sup>
mol<sup>1</sup> L<sup>−1</sup>
mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: General order-n units of k are mol<sup>1−n</sup>L<sup>n−1</sup>s<sup>−1</sup>. For n=1, the concentration part becomes mol<sup>0</sup>L<sup>0</sup> = 1, leaving just s<sup>−1</sup> — first order is the only common order where k has no concentration units at all, purely time inverse.
questions.hint: First-order k is the odd one out: it never has any concentration units, only s<sup>−1</sup>.
distractor_logic: Gives the units appropriate for a second-order reaction instead of first order.
Gives a set of units with no time dimension at all, which cannot be correct for any rate constant.
Gives the units appropriate for a zero-order reaction, where k does carry concentration units.

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A plot of ln[A] (or log<sub>10</sub>[A]) on the y-axis against time t for a first-order reaction gives:
options: an exponentially decaying curve, not a straight line
a straight line with slope −k (or −k/2.303 for log<sub>10</sub> base) and y-intercept ln[A]<sub>0</sub> (or log<sub>10</sub>[A]<sub>0</sub>)
a straight line, but only if [A] is plotted directly (not its logarithm) against time
a straight line with a positive slope equal to k
questions.explanation: Rearranging ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt into y = mx + c form: y = ln[A], x = t, slope = −k, intercept = ln[A]₀. Taking the logarithm of concentration is exactly what converts the exponential decay curve into a straight line for a first-order reaction.
questions.hint: Plotting the LOGARITHM of concentration (not concentration itself) against time gives the straight line for first order.
distractor_logic: Describes what a plot of [A] itself (not its logarithm) against time looks like for a first-order reaction; taking the log specifically straightens this exponential curve into a line.
Confuses first order with zero order; it is [A] itself (not its logarithm) that is linear in time for zero order, while ln[A] is linear in time for first order.
Gets the wrong sign for the slope; since [A] decreases with time, ln[A] must also decrease, giving a negative slope, not positive.

questions.question: For a first-order reaction, if the initial concentration of the reactant is doubled, what happens to the INITIAL RATE of the reaction (not the half-life)?

The initial rate becomes one-quarter of its original value
The initial rate quadruples

questions.question: A first-order reaction has k = 6.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> and [A]<sub>0</sub> = 1.00 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. What is [A] after 100 s?

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: In a first-order reaction, 75% of the initial amount of A decomposes in 138.2 s. Calculate the rate constant k.

5.43 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
7.50 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>

questions.hint: Always convert 'percentage decomposed' into 'fraction remaining' first ([A]/[A]₀), since the formula needs the remaining ratio, not the reacted one.
distractor_logic: Correctly identifies the ratio [A]<sub>0</sub>/[A] = 4 but then doubles the final k value through a stray extra factor of 2.
Uses [A]<sub>0</sub>/[A] = 1/0.75 (the fraction decomposed itself) instead of the correct ratio 1/0.25 (based on the fraction REMAINING), understating the true concentration ratio.
Treats 75% decomposed as meaning k simply equals 0.75 divided by t, skipping the logarithmic relation altogether.

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: For a first-order reaction, the following data was recorded: [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.900 mol L<sup>−1</sup> at t = 0 s; [A] = 0.450 mol L<sup>−1</sup> at t = 50 s; [A] = 0.225 mol L<sup>−1</sup> at t = 100 s. Verify the reaction is first order using this data, and predict [A] at t = 150 s.
options: k = 1.39 × 10<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> in the first interval but a different value in the second, so the reaction is NOT first order; extrapolation is unreliable
k = 1.39 × 10<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; [A] at 150 s = 0.150 mol L<sup>−1</sup> (assuming linear, not exponential, continuation)
k = 1.39 × 10<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> in BOTH intervals (confirming first order); [A] at 150 s = 0.1125 mol L<sup>−1</sup>
k cannot be verified without more data points; [A] at 150 s = 0.1125 mol L<sup>−1</sup> by simple visual pattern continuation alone
questions.explanation: k(0→50s) = (2.303/50)log(0.900/0.450) = (2.303/50)(0.301) = 1.39×10<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. k(50→100s) = (2.303/50)log(0.450/0.225) = same value, 1.39×10<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. Since k is identical in both intervals, the reaction is confirmed first order. Because each successive 50 s interval halves the concentration (a first-order signature), [A] at 150 s = 0.225/2 = 0.1125 mol L<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: In first order, equal time intervals always produce the same MULTIPLICATIVE (not additive/linear) drop in concentration.
distractor_logic: Makes a computational error in one of the two intervals, wrongly concluding the k values disagree, when a correct recalculation shows they actually match exactly.

Correctly verifies first order but then extrapolates [A] at 150 s using a LINEAR continuation of the concentration drop (0.225−0.075=0.150) rather than the correct exponential (constant-ratio) continuation appropriate to first order.

Dismisses the need for computing k in each interval and instead just extends the numeric pattern by eye, which happens to give the right final number here but isn't a valid general method (and doesn't 'verify' anything).

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: For a first-order reaction with k = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, compare the instantaneous rate of the reaction at t = 100 s to the instantaneous rate at t = 300 s. What is the ratio rate(t=100s) : rate(t=300s)?
questions.explanation: For a first-order reaction, rate = k[A], so the ratio of rates at two times equals the ratio of concentrations at those times: rate<sub>1</sub>/rate<sub>2</sub> = [A]<sub>1</sub>/[A]<sub>2</sub> = 10<sup>k−t/2.303</sup> where −t = t<sub>2</sub>−t<sub>1</sub> = 200 s. This gives 10<sup>(2.0×10<sup>−3</sup>)(200)/2.303</sup> = 10<sup>0.4/2.303</sup> = 10<sup>0.1737</sup> ≈ 1.49. So the rate at 100 s is about 1.49 times the rate at 300 s.
questions.hint: Rate is proportional to concentration for first order, so a rate ratio can be found the same way as a concentration ratio — no need to compute either rate separately first.
distractor_logic: Wrongly assumes rate stays constant over time for a first-order reaction, confusing it with zero order, where rate genuinely doesn't change.
Squares the correct ratio (1.49² ≈ 2.23) by mistakenly combining the effect twice instead of once.
Uses only kt (without dividing by 2.303) as the exponent, understating how much the rate has actually fallen between the two times.

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: For a gas-phase first-order decomposition A(g) → B(g) + C(g), the total pressure starts at P<sub>0</sub> = 300 mmHg (pure A) and rises to P<sub>t</sub> = 400 mmHg after 100 s. Find the partial pressure of A remaining at 100 s, and hence the rate constant k.
options: Partial pressure of A remaining = 200 mmHg; k = 4.06 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
Partial pressure of A remaining = 200 mmHg; k = 2.303 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
Partial pressure of A remaining = 400 mmHg; k = 0 s<sup>−1</sup> (no reaction has occurred)
Partial pressure of A remaining = 100 mmHg; k = 6.93 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: Let x = pressure of A that has reacted. Since 1 mol A gives 1 mol B + 1 mol C, P<sub>t</sub> = (P<sub>0</sub>−x) + x + x = P<sub>0</sub> + x, so x = P<sub>t</sub>−P<sub>0</sub> = 400−300 = 100 mmHg. Partial pressure of A remaining = P<sub>0</sub>−x = 300−100 = 200 mmHg. Then k = (2.303/100) log<sub>10</sub>(300/200) = (2.303/100)(0.176) = 4.06 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: For A(g)→B(g)+C(g) with 1:1:1 stoichiometry, each unit of pressure gained above P₀ corresponds to TWO units of A's own pressure having reacted away.
distractor_logic: Gets the pressure of A remaining correct but then forgets to multiply by 2.303 when computing k, using log₁₀ directly divided by t instead.
Wrongly assumes the total pressure equals the partial pressure of unreacted A directly, ignoring that B and C also contribute to the rising total pressure.

Mistakes the pressure INCREASE (P<sub>t</sub>−P<sub>0</sub>=100 mmHg) for the partial pressure of A remaining, rather than correctly subtracting that increase (twice, once for each product) from P<sub>0</sub>.

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A pollutant in a lake degrades by first-order kinetics with half-life 30 days, starting at an initial concentration of 40 ppm. Find the time taken to reduce the concentration to 10 ppm, and the ADDITIONAL time required (beyond that) to further reduce it all the way down to 2.5 ppm.
options: 60.0 days to reach 10 ppm; a further 120.0 days to reach 2.5 ppm
60.0 days to reach 10 ppm; a further 30.0 days to reach 2.5 ppm
30.0 days to reach 10 ppm; a further 30.0 days to reach 2.5 ppm
60.0 days to reach 10 ppm; a further 60.0 days (i.e. another 60 days) to reach 2.5 ppm
questions.explanation: k = 0.693/30 = 0.0231 day<sup>−1</sup>. Time to reach 10 ppm (a 4-fold drop from 40, i.e. 2 half-lives): t = (2.303/0.0231) log<sub>10</sub>(40/10) = 100 × log<sub>10</sub>(4) = 100 × 0.602 ≈ 60.0 days. Time to reach 2.5 ppm (a 16-fold drop from 40, i.e. 4 half-lives): t = 100 × log<sub>10</sub>(16) = 100 × 1.204 ≈ 120.0 days. Additional time beyond the first stage = 120.0 − 60.0 = 60.0 days — the SAME as the first stage, because reducing by the same multiplicative factor (4× here) always takes the same amount of time in first-order kinetics, regardless of the starting point.
questions.hint: A first-order reaction takes equal time for every equal MULTIPLICATIVE reduction, not just for halving — the 'quarter-life' is constant too, just like the half-life.
distractor_logic: Overestimates the second stage, perhaps by mistakenly adding an extra unwarranted doubling to the correctly-found first stage.

Correctly finds the first stage but then treats the second stage (a further 4-fold reduction, from 10 to 2.5 ppm) as if it only needed one more half-life, when it actually needs two more half-lives, i.e. the same total time as the first stage.
Confuses 'time for a 4-fold reduction' (two half-lives) with a single half-life, understating the first stage by exactly half.

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A first-order reaction has k = 1.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> at 300 K and k = 5.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> at 320 K. Find the activation energy, and use it to predict k at 340 K.
options: E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 32.1 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>; k at 340 K ≈ 1.02 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 64.2 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>; k at 340 K ≈ 2.07 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 64.2 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>; k at 340 K ≈ 5.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (unchanged, since the order of the reaction stays first order)
E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 64.2 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>; k at 340 K ≈ 9.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (extrapolated by simply continuing the same additive increase in k as before)
questions.explanation: log(k<sub>2</sub>/k<sub>1</sub>) = (E<sub>a</sub>/2.303R)(1/T<sub>1</sub>−1/T<sub>2</sub>): log(5.0×10<sup>−4</sup>/1.0×10<sup>−4</sup>) = log(5) = 0.699. 1/300−1/320 = 2.083×10<sup>−5</sup>. So E<sub>a</sub> = (2.303×8.314×0.699)/(2.083×10<sup>−5</sup>) ≈ 64,200 J mol<sup>−1</sup> = 64.2 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. Using k<sub>2</sub>=320K value as base to find k at 340K: log(k<sub>3</sub>/k<sub>2</sub>) = (E<sub>a</sub>/2.303R)(1/320−1/340) ≈ 0.617, so k<sub>3</sub> = 5.0×10<sup>−4</sup> × 10<sup>0.617</sup> ≈ 2.07 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: The order of a reaction (first order here) is a fixed label; the numerical value of k always keeps changing with temperature according to the Arrhenius equation, regardless of order.
distractor_logic: Halves E<sub>a</sub>, perhaps through a factor-of-2 slip in the two-temperature formula, and then propagates that smaller (wrong) E<sub>a</sub> into an equally understated k at 340 K.

Correctly finds E<sub>a</sub> but then wrongly assumes k must stay constant beyond 320 K just because the reaction's ORDER doesn't change with temperature — order and the numerical value of k are unrelated in this sense; k always keeps changing with T according to the Arrhenius equation.

Extrapolates k LINEARLY (adding the same 4.0×10<sup>−4</sup> increase again) instead of using the exponential Arrhenius relation, which is the same kind of linear-vs-exponential error as applying a zero-order formula to first-order-style temperature dependence.

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: The acidic hydrolysis of an ester, CH<sub>3</sub>COOC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH, is truly second order (first order in ester, first order in water), but water is used in such large excess (55.5 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, effectively constant) that the reaction is observed to follow first-order (pseudo-first-order) kinetics with measured k' = 1.1 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. What is the true second-order rate constant?
options: 1.98 × 10<sup>−5</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (correct number, but with first-order units left unchanged)
1.1 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> L s<sup>−1</sup> (same numeric value, just relabelled with second-order units)
6.11 × 10<sup>−2</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> L s<sup>−1</sup>
1.98 × 10<sup>−5</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> L s<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: The pseudo-first-order constant relates to the true constant by k' = k<sub>2</sub>[H<sub>2</sub>O] (since [H<sub>2</sub>O] stays essentially constant throughout). So k<sub>2</sub> = k'/[H<sub>2</sub>O] = (1.1×10<sup>−3</sup>)/55.5 ≈ 1.98 × 10<sup>−5</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> L s<sup>−1</sup> — note the units MUST switch to second-order units once you've recovered the true rate constant, since the true reaction is second order overall even though it behaves observably as first order under these particular (excess-water) conditions.
questions.hint: A pseudo rate constant is only 'first order' in appearance; recovering the true constant requires dividing out the (large, constant) concentration that was hidden inside it, and updating the units accordingly.
distractor_logic: Correctly divides to get the right number but then keeps the (wrong) first-order units s<sup>−1</sup> instead of switching to the true second-order units, mol<sup>−1</sup>Ls<sup>−1</sup>, which must change because the true reaction is second order overall.

Treats the pseudo rate constant as if it were already the true rate constant, forgetting that the pseudo constant is conditional on a specific (large, roughly-constant) water concentration and must be divided out to recover the true constant.
Multiplies by [H<sub>2</sub>O] instead of dividing by it, moving in the wrong direction and giving too large a number.

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: A reaction gives the following [A] vs t data: t = 0 s, [A] = 0.500 mol L<sup>−1</sup>; t = 40 s, [A] = 0.250 mol L<sup>−1</sup>; t = 80 s, [A] = 0.125 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. Confirm the order using the half-life method, find k, and separately confirm the order is consistent with the units of k you obtain.
options: Half-life doubles from the first interval to the second (40 s then 80 s), suggesting a different order; k cannot be meaningfully computed without resolving this discrepancy first

Half-life is constant at 40 s, confirming first order; but k = 1.73 × 10<sup>−2</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, which would actually indicate zero order, creating a contradiction that should have been caught

Half-life is constant at 40 s across both intervals, confirming first order; k = 1.73 × 10<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, and its units (s<sup>−1</sup>, no concentration term) independently confirm first order
Half-life is constant at 40 s; k = 3.47 × 10<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, obtained by using ln<sub>2</sub> = 1 instead of the correct value 0.693 in t<sub>1/2</sub> = ln<sub>2</sub>/k
questions.explanation: From 0.500<sup></sup>→0.250 mol L<sup>−1</sup>: half-life = 40 s. From 0.250→0.125 mol L<sup>−1</sup>: half-life is again 40 s (since 0.125 is exactly half of 0.250). A CONSTANT half-life, independent of the starting concentration within the interval, is the defining signature of first order. k = 0.693/40 = 1.73×10<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. The units (pure s<sup>−1</sup>, no concentration term at all) independently confirm this is a first-order reaction, since only first order gives k these units.
questions.hint: Two independent checks — half-life constancy AND the units of k — should always agree with each other; if they don't, recheck your arithmetic.
distractor_logic: Misreads the data: the half-life from 0.500→0.250 (40 s) and from 0.250→0.125 (again 40 s, since 0.125 is half of 0.250) are actually equal, not doubling — this option incorrectly claims they differ.

Correctly identifies the constant half-life (a genuine first-order signature) but then assigns the WRONG units to k, describing units that would actually belong to zero order — an internal inconsistency that a careful check should catch.
Uses an incorrect (too small) value for ln2 in the half-life-to-k conversion, roughly doubling the correct k value.

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: An uncatalysed first-order reaction has activation energy E<sub>a</sub> = 60 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. A catalyst lowers the activation energy to 50 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> without changing the pre-exponential factor A or the temperature (300 K). By what factor does the rate constant k increase due to the catalyst?
options: ≈ 55-fold increase
10-fold increase (equal to the drop in activation energy in kJ mol⁻¹)
1.2-fold increase (equal to the ratio 60/50 of the two activation energies)
No change in k, since a catalyst only changes the mechanism, not the numerical rate constant
questions.explanation: k = Ae<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>, so k<sub>catalysed</sub>/k<sub>uncatalysed</sub> = e<sup>(Ea,uncat−Ea,cat)/RT</sup> = e<sup>(60000−50000)/(8.314×300)</sup> = e<sup>10000/2494.2</sup> = e<sup>4.009</sup> ≈ 55. A relatively modest-looking 10 kJ/mol drop in activation energy produces a dramatic, exponential increase in rate — this is exactly why even small changes in activation energy (via catalysts) have such large practical effects on reaction rate.
questions.hint: The Arrhenius equation makes k depend EXPONENTIALLY on E<sub>a</sub> — never estimate the effect of a change in E<sub>a</sub> using simple ratios or differences.
distractor_logic: Mistakes the raw ARITHMETIC difference in E<sub>a</sub> (10 kJ/mol) for the multiplicative factor by which k changes, when the Arrhenius equation relates E<sub>a</sub> to k exponentially, not linearly.
Takes the simple ratio of the two E<sub>a</sub> values (60/50) as if k depended linearly on E<sub>a</sub>, instead of exponentially through k = Ae<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>.

Confuses 'a catalyst provides a new mechanism/pathway' with 'a catalyst doesn't change the measurable rate constant' — in fact, lowering the activation energy is EXACTLY what a catalyst does to increase k.

questions.topic: First Order Reactions and Integrated Rate Law
questions.question: Initial-rate data for a reaction A → products: at [A] = 0.10 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, rate = 2.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; at [A] = 0.20 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, rate = 4.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. Confirm the reaction is first order, find k, and use it to find the time needed for [A] to fall from 0.30 mol L<sup>−1</sup> to 0.075 mol L<sup>−1</sup>.
options: First order confirmed (rate doubles when [A] doubles); k = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; time = 693 s
First order confirmed; k = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; time = 346 s (using only one half-life instead of recognising two are needed)

Second order confirmed (since the rate values look proportionally consistent with [A]<sup>2</sup> for these particular numbers); k = 2.0 × 10<sup>−2</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> L s<sup>−1</sup>; time = 693 s
First order confirmed; k = 4.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (using the second data pair's rate instead of the ratio-based determination); time = 346 s
questions.explanation: Doubling [A] (0.10→0.20) doubles the rate (2.0→4.0, both ×10<sup>−4</sup>), confirming first order (rate ∝ [A]<sup>1</sup>). k = rate/[A] = (2.0×10<sup>−4</sup>)/0.10 = 2.0×10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. For 0.30→0.075 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, the ratio [A]<sub>0</sub>/[A] = 4, i.e. two half-lives: t = (2.303/k) log<sub>10</sub>(4) = (2.303/2.0×10<sup>−3</sup>)(0.602) ≈ 693 s.
questions.hint: For first order, k = rate/[A] at ANY single data point (not just the ratio method) — use whichever data point is convenient once order is confirmed.
distractor_logic: Correctly identifies first order and k but then only accounts for ONE half-life's worth of decay (0.30→0.15) instead of recognising that 0.30→0.075 is a 4-fold drop, requiring TWO half-lives.

Misapplies the initial-rate method, incorrectly concluding second order from data that actually shows a clean doubling-with-doubling (first-order) pattern, not the quadrupling that second order would require.
Uses the ratio rate/[A] from the WRONG data pair inconsistently or double-counts a factor, and separately underestimates the required decay time as in the first error.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: The half-life of a reaction is defined as:
options: the time required for the concentration of a reactant to fall to exactly half of its initial value
the time at which the rate of the forward reaction exactly equals the rate of the reverse reaction
the total time available for a reaction to occur before it is quenched
the time required for a reaction to reach completion (all reactant fully consumed)
questions.explanation: Half-life, t<sub>1/2</sub>, is the time taken for [A] to drop from [A]<sub>0</sub> to exactly [A]<sub>0</sub>/2 — a specific, well-defined point during the reaction's progress, not its full completion.
questions.hint: Half-life is about reaching the HALFWAY point in concentration, not finishing the reaction.
distractor_logic: Confuses half-life with the establishment of chemical equilibrium, which is a completely different concept.
Invents an operational definition unrelated to the standard kinetic meaning of half-life.
Confuses half-life with total completion time; half-life refers only to the concentration reaching half its starting value, not the reactant being fully used up.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: For a first-order reaction, the half-life:
options: is given by t<sub>1/2</sub> = [A]<sub>0</sub>/2k, and depends directly on the initial concentration
is given by t<sub>1/2</sub> = 0.693/k, and is completely independent of the initial concentration of the reactant
is not a meaningful concept for first-order reactions, since they never truly reach exactly half concentration
depends on the initial concentration, but in an inverse (not direct) proportional way
questions.explanation: For first order, t<sub>1/2</sub> = 0.693/k comes directly from the integrated rate law and contains no concentration term at all — this concentration-independence is one of the most distinctive and frequently tested features of first-order kinetics.
questions.hint: This concentration-independence of half-life is UNIQUE to first order among the common reaction orders.
distractor_logic: States the zero-order half-life formula, incorrectly applying it to first order.
Wrongly claims first-order reactions can't have a well-defined half-life; in fact first order is the classic case where half-life is not just meaningful but constant throughout the whole reaction.
Invents an inverse-proportionality relationship between half-life and initial concentration that does not exist for first order (the correct relationship is: no dependence at all).

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: For a zero-order reaction, the half-life:
options: is given by t<sub>1/2</sub> = 0.693/k, and is independent of the initial concentration
is always exactly equal to the half-life of an equivalent first-order reaction with the same numerical value of k
cannot be defined mathematically for a zero-order reaction, since the rate never changes
is given by t<sub>1/2</sub> = [A]<sub>0</sub>/2k, and is directly proportional to the initial concentration
questions.explanation: Setting [A]=[A]<sub>0</sub>/2 in [A]=[A]<sub>0</sub>−kt gives t<sub>1/2</sub>=[A]<sub>0</sub>/2k — unlike first order, this DOES depend on the initial concentration (doubling [A]₀ doubles the half-life).
questions.hint: Zero-order half-life is the exact opposite of first-order half-life in this respect: it depends directly on [A]₀.
distractor_logic: States the first-order half-life formula, incorrectly applying it to zero order.
Wrongly assumes half-life formulas from different orders coincide just because k has the same numerical value; the formulas themselves (and hence the resulting half-lives) are structurally different.
Wrongly assumes a constant rate means half-life is undefined; a zero-order reaction still has a perfectly well-defined (and easily derived) half-life, t<sub>1/2</sub>=[A]<sub>0</sub>/2k.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: For a first-order reaction, if the half-life is 40 seconds, what fraction of the reactant remains after three successive half-lives (120 seconds total)?
options: 1/2 (since half-life by definition always leaves half remaining, no matter how many pass)
questions.explanation: Each half-life halves whatever concentration remains at its start: after 1 half-life, 1/2 remains; after 2, 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 remains; after 3, 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8 remains. In general, after n half-lives, the fraction remaining is (1/2)ⁿ.
questions.hint: Multiply by 1/2 repeatedly, once per half-life — never simply divide the original fraction by the number of half-lives.
distractor_logic: Misapplies the definition of a single half-life to ALL elapsed time, forgetting that each successive half-life halves whatever fraction remained at the START of that particular interval.
Wrongly divides the fraction remaining linearly by the number of half-lives (1/3) instead of applying the halving repeatedly (multiplicatively).
Makes an arithmetic slip combining the number of half-lives with the fraction in a way that doesn't reflect repeated halving.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares the half-life behaviour of zero-order and first-order reactions?
options: Both zero-order and first-order half-lives are always independent of the initial concentration
Both zero-order and first-order half-lives always increase as the initial concentration is decreased
Zero-order half-life is independent of initial concentration, while first-order half-life depends directly on it
Zero-order half-life shortens as the initial concentration is decreased, while first-order half-life stays exactly the same no matter how the initial concentration is chosen
questions.explanation: First-order t<sub>1/2</sub>=0.693/k has no [A]<sub>0</sub> term at all (constant regardless of starting concentration). Zero-order t<sub>1/2</sub>=[A]<sub>0</sub>/2k is directly proportional to [A]<sub>0</sub>, so a smaller starting concentration gives a proportionally shorter half-life.
questions.hint: Remember which formula contains [A]₀ and which doesn't — that alone tells you which order depends on starting concentration.
distractor_logic: Wrongly extends the (correct, but order-specific) first-order independence property to zero order as well, when zero order explicitly does depend on initial concentration.
Gets the DIRECTION backwards for zero order: decreasing [A]₀ actually shortens (not lengthens) the zero-order half-life, since half-life is directly, not inversely, proportional to [A]₀.
Swaps which order has which property — it is zero order that depends on [A]₀, and first order that does not.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A first-order reaction has k = 4.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. What is its half-life?
questions.hint: This is a direct one-line substitution into t⅓₂ = 0.693/k — no other data is needed for first order.
distractor_logic: Divides the correct answer by 2 again, as if an extra halving were needed beyond the standard t<sub>1/2</sub>=0.693/k formula.
Doubles the correct answer, perhaps by using t<sub>1/2</sub>=2(0.693)/k instead of 0.693/k.
Uses ln3 (≈1.0986, relevant to a different fraction) in place of ln2 (0.693) in the half-life formula.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 346.5 s. What is its rate constant k?
options: 6.93 × 10<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
1.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
4.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: k = 0.693/t<sub>1/2</sub> = 0.693/346.5 = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Simply rearrange t<sub>1/2</sub>=0.693/k to k=0.693/t<sub>1/2</sub>.
distractor_logic: Reports 0.693 divided by nothing (i.e. forgets to actually divide by the half-life value at all).
Doubles the denominator unnecessarily in the rearranged formula, halving the resulting k a second, different way.
Halves the correct k, perhaps by using k=0.693/(2×t<sub>1/2</sub>) instead of the correct k=0.693/t<sub>1/2</sub>.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 60 s. How long will it take for the reaction to reach 87.5% completion (i.e. only 12.5% of the reactant remains)?
questions.explanation: 12.5% remaining = 1/8 = (1/2)³, i.e. exactly 3 half-lives have passed. t = 3 × t⅓₂ = 3 × 60 = 180 s.
questions.hint: Express the remaining fraction as a power of 1/2 first — the exponent directly tells you the number of half-lives.
distractor_logic: Assumes 87.5% completion corresponds to only 2 half-lives (25% remaining) instead of correctly recognising 12.5% remaining requires 3 half-lives.
Uses a non-integer, incorrectly interpolated number of half-lives instead of recognising that 12.5% = (1/2)³ corresponds to exactly 3 whole half-lives.
Overshoots by assuming 4 half-lives (6.25% remaining) are needed instead of the correct 3.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 25 s. How long will it take for 93.75% of the reactant to decompose?
questions.explanation: 93.75% decomposed means 6.25% remains = 1/16 = (1/2)⁴, i.e. exactly 4 half-lives. t = 4 × 25 = 100 s.
questions.hint: 6.25% is (1/2) to the 4th power — always convert the remaining percentage into a clean fraction first.
distractor_logic: Assumes 93.75% decomposition needs only 3 half-lives (87.5% decomposed) instead of the correct 4 half-lives.
Overshoots to 5 half-lives instead of the correct 4.
Uses a non-power-of-2 interpolation between half-life multiples instead of recognising the clean 4-half-life relationship.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A zero-order reaction and a first-order reaction both have [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.50 mol L<sup>−1</sup> and the same numerical rate constant value, k = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> (in each reaction's own appropriate units). Compare their half-lives.
options: Zero-order half-life = 346.5 s; first-order half-life = 125 s (the two values swapped relative to their correct formulas)
Both half-lives are exactly equal (125 s), since k has the same numerical value in both cases
Zero-order half-life = 125 s; first-order half-life ≈ 346.5 s — they are different, since the two formulas have completely different structures
Both half-lives are exactly equal (346.5 s), since half-life only depends on k, regardless of order
questions.explanation: Zero order: t<sub>1/2</sub> = [A]<sub>0</sub>/2k = 0.50/(2×2.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 125 s. First order: t<sub>1/2</sub> = 0.693/k = 0.693/(2.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 346.5 s. Even with the 'same' numerical k, the half-lives differ substantially, because k for different orders isn't even directly comparable — it carries different units and enters a structurally different formula in each case.
questions.hint: Never assume k values are directly comparable across different orders — they have different units and appear in different formulas.
distractor_logic: Gets both individual half-life VALUES right but assigns them to the wrong order, mixing up which formula belongs to which reaction type.

Wrongly assumes equal numerical k automatically means equal half-lives, ignoring that the two formulas ([A]<sub>0</sub>/2k vs 0.693/k) are structurally different and even carry different UNITS for k, making a naive numeric comparison invalid to begin with.
Makes the same equal-half-life assumption, just landing on the first-order value instead, still ignoring that the formulas (and units of k) genuinely differ between orders.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 50 s. How long will it take for the concentration to fall to 30% of its initial value (i.e. 70% decomposed)? (This does not correspond to a whole number of half-lives, so use the integrated rate law directly.)
questions.explanation: First, k = 0.693/50 = 0.01386 s<sup>−1</sup>. Since 30% is not a clean power of 1/2, use the full logarithmic relation: t = (2.303/k) log<sub>10</sub>(1/0.30) = (2.303/0.01386)(0.523) ≈ 86.9 s. This sits sensibly between 1 half-life (50 s, 50% remaining) and 2 half-lives (100 s, 25% remaining), since 30% remaining lies between those two benchmarks.
questions.hint: When the target fraction isn't a clean power of 1/2, fall back on the general logarithmic formula rather than counting half-lives.
distractor_logic: Makes an arithmetic slip in converting log₁₀(1/0.30) into time, overestimating the result.
Assumes roughly 3 half-lives are needed (as if 30% were close enough to round down to 12.5%), overshooting substantially.

Wrongly assumes the answer must fall between 1 and 2 half-lives via simple linear interpolation (e.g. treating 30% remaining as 70% of the way from 1 to 2 half-lives) rather than actually using the logarithmic relation.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A first-order reaction proceeds through 6 successive half-lives. What percentage of the original reactant remains unreacted, and what percentage has decomposed?
options: 1.5625% remains; 98.4375% has decomposed
0.78125% remains; 99.21875% has decomposed
6.25% remains; 93.75% has decomposed
3.125% remains; 96.875% has decomposed
questions.explanation: Fraction remaining after n half-lives = (1/2)ⁿ. For n=6: (1/2)⁶ = 1/64 = 0.015625, i.e. 1.5625% remains. Percentage decomposed = 100 − 1.5625 = 98.4375%.
questions.hint: Compute (1/2) raised to the power equal to the number of half-lives, then convert that fraction to a percentage.
distractor_logic: Overcounts by exactly one half-life, giving the result appropriate for 7 half-lives instead of 6.
Undercounts by two half-lives, giving the result appropriate for 4 half-lives instead of 6.
Undercounts by exactly one half-life, giving the result appropriate for 5 half-lives instead of 6.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: Two first-order reactions, P and Q, have half-lives of 20 s and 35 s respectively. Which reaction takes longer to reach 90% completion (10% remaining), and by how much?
options: Reaction Q takes longer, by approximately 49.8 s (Q takes ≈116.3 s, P takes ≈66.5 s)
Reaction Q takes longer, by approximately 15 s (simply the difference in their half-lives)
Both reactions take exactly the same time to reach 90% completion, since the target percentage is the same for both
Reaction P takes longer, by approximately 49.8 s
questions.explanation: k<sub>P</sub> = 0.693/20 = 0.03465 s<sup>−1</sup>; k<sub>Q</sub> = 0.693/35 = 0.0198 s<sup>−1</sup>. Time to 90% completion (10% remaining, ratio 10): t<sub>P</sub> = (2.303/0.03465)log<sub>10</sub>(10) = 66.5 s; t<sub>Q</sub> = (2.303/0.0198)log<sub>10</sub>(10) = 116.3 s. Q (the slower reaction, longer half-life) takes about 49.8 s longer to reach 90% completion.
questions.hint: A longer half-life always means a smaller k, which always means MORE time is needed to reach any given percentage completion.
distractor_logic: Assumes the difference in time to reach 90% completion simply equals the difference in half-lives, when in fact the time scales with (2.303/k), not linearly with t⅓₂ differences alone.

Wrongly assumes reaching the 'same percentage completion' takes the same absolute time regardless of the reactions' different rate constants; the target fraction being the same does not mean the required time is the same, since the underlying k values differ.

Gets the direction backwards; the reaction with the LONGER half-life (Q, larger t⅓₂, smaller k) necessarily takes longer to reach any given percentage completion, not the one with the shorter half-life.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A first-order reaction is found to be 60% complete in 120 s. Find its half-life, and hence predict how much longer (beyond this first 120 s) it would take to reach 90% completion overall.
options: t<sub>1/2</sub> ≈ 90.7 s; a further exactly 90.7 s is needed (i.e. exactly one more half-life gets you from 60% to 90% completion)
t<sub>1/2</sub> ≈ 60.0 s (simply reading the given completion percentage as if it directly gave the half-life)
t<sub>1/2</sub> ≈ 120 s (assuming 120 s and 60% completion must define the half-life directly, without any calculation)
t<sub>1/2</sub> ≈ 90.7 s; the reaction needs a further ≈181.6 s beyond the first 120 s (total time to 90% completion ≈ 301.6 s)
questions.explanation: k = (2.303/120) log<sub>10</sub>(1/0.40) = (2.303/120)(0.398) ≈ 7.64×10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. t<sub>1/2</sub> = 0.693/k ≈ 90.7 s. Total time to 90% completion (10% remaining): t = (2.303/k) log<sub>10</sub>(1/0.10) = (2.303/7.64×10<sup>−3</sup>)(1) ≈ 301.6 s. Additional time beyond the first 120 s = 301.6 − 120 ≈ 181.6 s.
questions.hint: First recover k (or t⅓₂) from the given data point, then use it fresh to calculate the NEW total time needed — don't assume round numbers of half-lives apply between arbitrary percentages.
distractor_logic: Correctly finds the half-life but then wrongly assumes reaching 60%→90% completion takes exactly one more half-life, when the relationship between these specific completion percentages doesn't correspond to a clean whole number of half-lives at all.
Confuses the raw given percentage (60%) with the half-life value itself, skipping the actual kinetic calculation entirely.
Confuses the given time (120 s) with the half-life directly, ignoring that 120 s corresponds to 60% completion, not 50%.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 100 s at 300 K. If its activation energy is E<sub>a</sub> = 50 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, estimate its half-life at 320 K.
options: ≈ 28.6 s
≈ 371.4 s (a longer half-life, mistakenly assuming raising the temperature slows the reaction down)
≈ 50.0 s (half-life simply scales down by the same 20 K / 20-degree-doubling heuristic used for rate)
≈ 100 s (unchanged, since half-life for a first-order reaction never depends on any external condition)
questions.explanation: k<sub>1</sub> = 0.693/100 = 6.93×10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> at 300 K. Using the Arrhenius two-temperature form: log(k<sub>2</sub>/k<sub>1</sub>) = (E<sub>a</sub>/2.303R)(1/300−1/320) ≈ 0.544, so k<sub>2</sub> ≈ 6.93×10<sup>−3</sup> × 10<sup>0.544</sup> ≈ 0.0243 s<sup>−1</sup>. New half-life = 0.693/0.0243 ≈ 28.6 s — substantially shorter, since even a 20 K rise noticeably speeds up the reaction.
questions.hint: First-order half-life's independence from CONCENTRATION does not mean independence from TEMPERATURE — always recompute k via Arrhenius before converting to a new half-life.
distractor_logic: Gets the direction of the temperature effect completely backwards; raising temperature always increases k and therefore always DECREASES half-life, never increases it.

Applies a rough 'doubles per 10°C' heuristic (a factor of 4 for 20°) directly to t<sub>1/2</sub> instead of properly recalculating k from the Arrhenius equation at the new temperature and then converting to t<sub>1/2</sub>.

Wrongly extends 'half-life is independent of INITIAL CONCENTRATION' to mean 'half-life is independent of everything', when temperature (through the Arrhenius equation's effect on k) absolutely does change t<sub>1/2</sub>.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A reaction is studied at two different starting concentrations. At [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.80 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, the half-life is 50 s. At [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.40 mol L<sup>−1</sup> (half the concentration), the half-life is found to be 100 s (double). What is the order of the reaction?
options: Second order (order = 2)
First order, since half-life changes are always associated with first-order reactions
Order cannot be determined from half-life data of this kind, only from initial-rate data
Zero order, since the half-life changed when the concentration changed
questions.explanation: For a reaction of order n, half-life relates to initial concentration as t<sub>1/2</sub> ∝ [A]<sub>0</sub><sup>1−n</sup>. Halving [A]₀ (a factor of 0.5) DOUBLED the half-life (a factor of 2). Solving 2 = (0.5)<sup>1−n</sup>: taking logs, log2 = (1−n)log(0.5), so (1−n) = log2/log0.5 = −1, giving n = 2. This inverse relationship (half-life increases as concentration decreases) is the signature of second order, opposite to zero order (where half-life increases as concentration INCREASES).
questions.hint: Compare the DIRECTION of the relationship: half-life rising as concentration falls signals second order; half-life rising as concentration rises signals zero order; no change at all signals first order.
distractor_logic: Confuses 'half-life changed with concentration' with first order, when the defining feature of first order is precisely the OPPOSITE: constant half-life regardless of concentration.
Wrongly dismisses the half-life method entirely; comparing half-lives at different starting concentrations is in fact a standard, valid way to determine reaction order.

Correctly notices the half-life is concentration-dependent (ruling out first order) but stops short of using the specific pattern (inverse proportionality) to correctly identify second order, guessing zero order (which would show DIRECT, not inverse, proportionality) instead.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: The pseudo-first-order hydrolysis of an ester (with water in large excess) has a measured pseudo rate constant k' = 1.155 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. What is the half-life of the ester's disappearance under these conditions?
questions.explanation: Even though the TRUE reaction is second order overall, under pseudo-first-order conditions it behaves exactly like a first-order reaction with respect to the ester, so the ordinary first-order half-life formula applies directly to k': t<sub>1/2</sub> = 0.693/k' = 0.693/(1.155×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 600 s.
questions.hint: Under pseudo-first-order conditions, treat k' exactly like an ordinary first-order rate constant for half-life purposes.
distractor_logic: Reports the value of 0.693/k' with an incorrect numerator (using 0.8 instead of 0.693, or a similar constant mix-up).
Halves the correct value, perhaps by using t<sub>1/2</sub>=0.693/(2k') instead of the correct 0.693/k'.
Doubles the correct value, perhaps by using t<sub>1/2</sub>=2×0.693/k' instead of 0.693/k'.

Pseudo First Order Reactions

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A first-order reaction has [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.40 mol L<sup>−1</sup> and k = 0.0139 s<sup>−1</sup> (t<sub>1/2</sub> ≈ 49.9 s). Compare the AVERAGE rate of the reaction during the FIRST half-life (t=0 to t=t<sub>1/2</sub>) with the average rate during the SECOND half-life (t=t<sub>1/2</sub> to t=2t<sub>1/2</sub>).
options: The average rate during the second half-life is double that of the first, since the reaction speeds up as it nears completion
This comparison is meaningless because average rate can only be defined for the very first instant of a reaction

Average rate during the first half-life ≈ 4.01 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, exactly DOUBLE the average rate during the second half-life (≈ 2.01 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>), even though both intervals last the same amount of time
Both average rates are exactly equal, since the half-life (a fixed time interval) is the same length for both
questions.explanation: First half-life (0.40→0.20 mol L<sup>−1</sup> over 49.9 s): average rate = 0.20/49.9 ≈ 4.01×10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. Second half-life (0.20→0.10 mol L<sup>−1</sup> over the SAME 49.9 s): average rate = 0.10/49.9 ≈ 2.01×10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. Even though both intervals last exactly one half-life (equal TIME), the average rate halves from one interval to the next, because a smaller amount of A is being consumed in the second, equal-length interval — this is very different from zero order, where average rate would stay exactly constant across successive equal-length intervals.
questions.hint: For first order, equal TIME intervals do NOT give equal average rates — only equal MULTIPLICATIVE drops in concentration take equal time.
distractor_logic: Gets the direction of the change backwards; a first-order reaction SLOWS DOWN (not speeds up) as it proceeds, because rate = k[A] and [A] keeps falling — so later intervals have smaller average rates, not larger ones.
Wrongly claims average rate is undefined beyond the first instant; average rate is perfectly well-defined over ANY chosen time interval, using Δ[A]/Δt.

Wrongly assumes equal TIME intervals must give equal average RATES; that would only be true for a zero-order reaction, not first order, where the concentration driving the rate keeps falling within each successive interval.

questions.topic: Half-life of a Reaction
questions.question: A zero-order reaction has [A]<sub>0</sub> = 0.80 mol L<sup>−1</sup> and k = 4.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. Find the first half-life (time for [A] to fall from 0.80 to 0.40), and then the NEXT half-life (time for [A] to fall from 0.40 to 0.20). How do these two successive half-lives compare?
options: First half-life = 100 s; second (next) half-life = 50 s — successive half-lives get shorter and shorter for a zero-order reaction, exactly the opposite of first order, where they would all stay equal
First half-life = 100 s; second half-life = 200 s (successive half-lives get LONGER for zero order)

This calculation is not meaningful because half-life for zero order is only defined once, starting from [A]<sub>0</sub>, and cannot be recalculated from a new starting point partway through the reaction
Both successive half-lives are exactly equal at 100 s each, just like they would be for a first-order reaction
questions.explanation: First half-life: t<sub>1/2</sub> = [A]<sub>0</sub>/2k = 0.80/(2×4.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 100 s. At this point [A] = 0.40 mol L<sup>−1</sup>; treating THIS as a fresh starting concentration, the next half-life = 0.40/(2×4.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) = 50 s. Because zero-order half-life is directly proportional to whatever concentration you start counting from, and that concentration keeps shrinking as the reaction proceeds, each successive half-life is exactly half as long as the one before it — the reverse of first order, where every half-life is identical regardless of starting point.
questions.hint: Re-apply the zero-order half-life formula fresh at each new starting concentration — unlike first order, it is NOT a single fixed number for the whole reaction.
distractor_logic: Gets the correct first value but then gets the DIRECTION of the trend backwards; since zero-order half-life is directly proportional to the current starting concentration, and that concentration is falling, successive half-lives must shrink, not grow.

Wrongly claims half-life can only be computed from the original [A]<sub>0</sub>; the half-life formula t<sub>1/2</sub>=[A]<sub>current</sub>/2k can validly be reapplied starting from ANY concentration reached during the reaction, not just the very first one.

Wrongly imports the first-order property (constant successive half-lives) into zero order, where half-life instead depends directly on whatever concentration remains at the start of each interval, and therefore keeps shrinking.
