questions.topic: Temperature Dependence of Rate: Arrhenius Equation and Activation Energy
questions.question: At T = 298 K, a reaction has E<sub>a</sub> = 45.0 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. Using collision theory's expression for the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub> (f = e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>), calculate this fraction, and explain why, despite billions of collisions occurring every second in a typical reacting mixture, the reaction still proceeds at a measurable, finite (not instantaneous) rate (R = 8.314 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>).
options: f ≈ 1.3×10<sup>−8</sup>; only this tiny fraction of the enormous number of collisions has enough energy to react (and, further, only some of those are also correctly oriented), so despite huge total collision numbers, only a very small absolute number of collisions are actually effective per second
f ≈ 1.3×10<sup>−8</sup>; the reaction proceeds slowly because collisions themselves are actually very rare events in any real reacting mixture, occurring far less often than commonly assumed
f ≈ 0.45 (mistakenly treating the given Ea value in kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> as if it were already the correct exponent, without converting to J mol<sup>−1</sup> or properly dividing by RT)

f ≈ 1.3×10<sup>−8</sup>; this fraction is irrelevant to the reaction's overall speed, since collision theory says total collision FREQUENCY alone determines rate, regardless of what fraction of those collisions have sufficient energy
questions.explanation: f = e<sup>−45000/(8.314×298)</sup> ≈ 1.3×10<sup>−8</sup>, meaning only about 1 in 77 million collisions has enough energy to overcome the activation barrier. Even though the ABSOLUTE number of collisions per second in a typical reacting system is enormous, multiplying that huge number by such a tiny fraction (and further reducing it by the steric/orientation factor) still yields a finite, measurable number of effective collisions per second, which is what determines the observed reaction rate.
questions.hint: The reaction rate depends on collision frequency MULTIPLIED BY the (typically very small) energy-sufficient fraction and orientation factor, not on collision frequency alone.
distractor_logic: Gets the underlying physical picture backwards; collision theory's whole premise is that molecular collisions in a typical gas or solution are actually extremely FREQUENT (many billions per second), not rare — it's the small fraction of those many collisions that are both energetic and properly oriented enough to react that limits the rate.

Fails to properly evaluate the exponential; simply using 45 (in kJ) instead of correctly converting to 45,000 J mol<sup>−1</sup> and dividing by RT≈2478 J mol<sup>−1</sup> produces a nonsensical result nowhere close to the correct tiny fraction.

Wrongly claims collision frequency alone determines rate; collision theory explicitly multiplies collision frequency by BOTH the energy-sufficient fraction and the steric (orientation) factor, and it is precisely this small energy-sufficient fraction that usually limits the rate far more than the raw collision count.

questions.question: A first-order reaction has k = 2.0×10<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> at a certain temperature. (a) Find its half-life. (b) A student argues that since order and molecularity are 'basically the same thing,' this first-order reaction must proceed through a single-molecule elementary step, and that this single-step nature is also why doubling the temperature would exactly double k. Identify every error in this reasoning.
options: (a) t½ = 0.693/k ≈ 34.65 s; (b) only the molecularity claim is an error; the claim about doubling T doubling k is actually correct, since the Arrhenius equation is a simple direct proportionality between k and T

(a) t½ = 0.693/k ≈ 34.65 s; (b) the reasoning is entirely correct, since a first-order rate law is definitionally the same as a one-molecule elementary mechanism, and the Arrhenius equation does predict that doubling absolute temperature exactly doubles k

(a) t½ = 0.693/k ≈ 34.65 s; (b) two separate errors: order (empirical) and molecularity (mechanistic, valid only for elementary steps) are NOT generally the same thing, and separately, k does not scale linearly with T at all — it follows the exponential Arrhenius relationship, so doubling T would not simply double k
(a) t½ = k/0.693 ≈ 0.029 s (formula inverted); (b) the reasoning has the errors described above
questions.explanation: (a) For a first-order reaction, t½ = 0.693/k = 0.693/(2.0×10<sup>−2</sup>) ≈ 34.65 s. (b) Two independent errors: first, order and molecularity coincide only for elementary (single-step) reactions, and a measured first order does not by itself prove a one-molecule mechanism; second, the Arrhenius equation shows k depends EXPONENTIALLY on T (via e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>), not linearly, so doubling the absolute temperature does not generally double k — the actual multiplicative factor depends on both E<sub>a</sub> and the specific temperature values involved.
questions.hint: Treat the half-life calculation, the order-vs-molecularity distinction, and the (exponential, not linear) Arrhenius temperature dependence as three separate checks.
distractor_logic: Correctly flags the molecularity error but wrongly endorses the temperature claim; k depends EXPONENTIALLY on T via the Arrhenius equation (through e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>), not through simple direct proportionality, so doubling absolute T does not generally double k — the actual factor depends on E<sub>a</sub> and the specific temperatures.

Wrongly endorses both flawed claims: order and molecularity coincide only for elementary reactions (not as a general rule), and the Arrhenius equation is exponential, not linear, in T — doubling T does NOT generally double k, and the actual factor depends on Ea and the specific temperatures involved.
Inverts the half-life formula; for a first-order reaction it is t½=0.693/k (giving ≈34.65 s), not k/0.693.

questions.question: For an elementary bimolecular reaction, the rate constant can be modelled as k = P×Z×e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>, where P is the steric (orientation) factor, Z is the collision frequency factor, and the exponential term is the energy-sufficient fraction. Given P = 0.50, Z = 1.0×10<sup>11</sup> L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, E<sub>a</sub> = 55.0 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, and T = 300 K, calculate k, and explain what role molecularity plays in this particular calculation (R = 8.314 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>).
options: k ≈ 13.3 L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; molecularity is irrelevant here, since the formula uses only P, Z, Ea, and T, none of which has anything to do with how many species are colliding
k ≈ 1.0×10<sup>11</sup> L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (forgetting to include both P and the exponential term, using Z alone as k)

k ≈ 13.3 L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; molecularity (bimolecular, i.e. two species colliding) is exactly why this collision-theory expression — with its collision-frequency term Z between two molecules — applies at all, since collision theory in this simple form is built around elementary steps with a defined number of colliding species
k ≈ 26.5 L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (forgetting to include the steric factor P, effectively assuming every correctly-energetic collision also has perfect orientation)
questions.explanation: k = P×Z×e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup> = 0.50×(1.0×10<sup>11</sup>)×e<sup>−55000/(8.314×300)</sup> ≈ 13.3 L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. This particular collision-theory expression, with its single well-defined collision-frequency term Z, is meaningful precisely because the reaction is elementary and bimolecular (molecularity = 2); collision theory in this simple two-body form does not directly apply to an overall reaction's empirical rate law unless that reaction actually proceeds as a single elementary bimolecular step.
questions.hint: The collision-theory rate expression (with a single Z term for two colliding species) presumes a defined molecularity; it's built specifically for elementary reactions.
distractor_logic: Wrongly claims molecularity plays no role; the entire premise of this collision-theory formula (a defined collision frequency Z between reacting species) is built on the reaction being a genuine elementary step with a specific, countable number of colliding molecules (here, bimolecular) — this equation would not be meaningfully applicable to an overall multi-step reaction's empirical order.
Uses only the collision frequency factor Z as if it were the full rate constant, omitting both the steric factor P and the energy-sufficient exponential term entirely.
Omits the steric factor P (0.50), effectively assuming every collision with sufficient energy is also perfectly oriented to react, which overstates k by a factor of 1/P = 2.

questions.topic: Effect of Catalyst on Reaction Rate
questions.question: A catalyst speeds up a reaction primarily by:
options: shifting the position of equilibrium further toward products
increasing the concentration of the reactants
providing an alternative reaction pathway (mechanism) with lower activation energy
increasing the temperature of the reacting mixture
questions.explanation: Catalysts work by offering a different, lower-energy mechanistic route from reactants to products, often via forming a temporary intermediate. Because this new pathway has a lower activation energy, a much larger fraction of molecules can now cross the barrier at any given temperature, increasing the rate.
questions.hint: Think of a catalyst as opening a lower 'mountain pass' between reactants and products, rather than making the reactants themselves more abundant or hotter.
distractor_logic: A catalyst does not shift the equilibrium position at all; it speeds up the approach to the same equilibrium, but does not favor products over reactants any more than it did without the catalyst.
A catalyst does not change how much reactant is present; it changes the PATHWAY by which reactants convert to products, not their amount.
A catalyst works without any change in temperature; the whole point of catalysis is achieving a faster rate at the SAME temperature, unlike simply heating the mixture.

questions.topic: Effect of Catalyst on Reaction Rate
questions.question: Which of the following statements about a catalyst is correct?
options: A catalyst speeds up only the forward reaction, never the reverse reaction
A catalyst is consumed during the reaction and must be continually replenished
A catalyst increases the equilibrium constant of the reaction, favoring more product formation
A catalyst speeds up both the forward and the reverse reaction equally, so it does not change the equilibrium constant
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount (since both pass through the same lower-energy transition state/intermediate), so it speeds up both directions equally. This means the equilibrium constant (which depends on the ratio of forward and reverse rate constants) is unaffected; only the TIME taken to reach equilibrium is reduced.
questions.hint: A catalyst changes the RATE at which equilibrium is reached, never the POSITION of equilibrium itself.
distractor_logic: Incorrect; because a catalyst lowers the activation energy of BOTH the forward and reverse pathways (by the same amount, since it affects the shared intermediate/transition state), it speeds up both directions, not just the forward one.
Incorrect; by definition, a true catalyst is regenerated at the end of the reaction cycle and is not consumed overall, even though it may take part in intermediate steps along the way.

Incorrect; since a catalyst affects forward and reverse rates identically, the ratio of forward to reverse rate constants at equilibrium (which defines the equilibrium constant) is unchanged — a catalyst only changes how FAST equilibrium is reached, not WHERE it lies.

questions.topic: Effect of Catalyst on Reaction Rate
questions.question: A catalyst lowers a reaction's activation energy from 65.0 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> to 50.0 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> at 298 K, with the pre-exponential factor A unchanged. By what factor does the rate constant increase (R = 8.314 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)?
options: By a factor of about 1.02 (mistakenly using Ea directly in kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> inside the exponent instead of correctly converting to J mol<sup>−1</sup> before dividing by RT)
By a factor of about 426
By a factor of exactly 15 000 (mistakenly treating the raw 15 kJ/mol difference in Ea, in J mol−1, directly as the multiplicative factor without exponentiating)
By a factor of about 1.3 (mistakenly taking the plain ratio 65/50 of the two Ea values as the rate factor)
questions.explanation: k(after)/k(before) = e<sup>[Ea(before)−Ea(after)]/RT</sup> = e<sup>15000/(8.314×298)</sup> ≈ e<sup>6.05</sup> ≈ 426. This shows how a comparatively modest 15 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> reduction in activation energy (well within the typical range achievable by good catalysts) can multiply the rate constant several hundredfold.
questions.hint: Use the exponential relationship between the CHANGE in Ea and the rate-constant ratio, being careful to work in consistent energy units (J, to match R).
distractor_logic: Fails to convert kJ to J before dividing by RT (which uses R in J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>), producing an exponent that is 1000× too small and hence a rate factor barely above 1.
Wrongly treats the raw energy difference (in J mol−1) as if it were already the rate factor itself, without passing it through the exponential.
Wrongly uses a plain ratio of the two Ea values instead of the correct exponential relationship k(after)/k(before)=e^[(Ea,before−Ea,after)/RT].

questions.topic: Effect of Catalyst on Reaction Rate
questions.question: A student proposes that adding a catalyst to a reaction that has already reached equilibrium will shift the equilibrium to produce more product, since the catalyst makes the forward reaction faster. Explain why this reasoning is flawed.
options: The reasoning is flawed because catalysts actually only ever speed up the reverse reaction, never the forward one, so the equilibrium would shift toward MORE reactant, not more product

The catalyst speeds up the reverse reaction by exactly the same factor as the forward reaction (both pass through the same lowered-energy pathway), so the system reaches the SAME equilibrium position faster, with no net shift toward either products or reactants
The reasoning is correct; making the forward reaction faster while leaving the reverse reaction's rate unchanged necessarily produces more product overall
The reasoning is flawed only because a catalyst added AFTER equilibrium is reached has no effect on the system at all, unlike one added before the reaction starts
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse pathways by the same amount, since both directions pass through the identical (lower-energy) transition state or intermediate that the catalyst provides. This means the forward and reverse rate constants both increase by the same multiplicative factor, leaving their RATIO (the equilibrium constant) — and hence the equilibrium position — completely unchanged; only the time needed to reach that same equilibrium position is shortened.
questions.hint: Whatever pathway the catalyst opens up is shared by both the forward and reverse reactions, so both speed up together, leaving equilibrium position untouched.
distractor_logic: Gets the catalyst's effect on direction completely backwards; a catalyst does not selectively favor only the reverse direction — it speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, regardless of when it's introduced.

Wrongly assumes only the forward rate changes; in reality both forward and reverse rates increase by the same factor (since the catalyst lowers the activation energy of both directions equally), so there is no net shift in equilibrium position.

Incorrectly claims catalysts added after equilibrium do nothing; in fact a catalyst added at any point (before or after equilibrium is reached) speeds up the approach to the SAME equilibrium state, it just does so from wherever the system currently stands.

questions.topic: Effect of Catalyst on Reaction Rate
questions.question: For an uncatalyzed reaction, E<sub>a</sub>(forward) = 80 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> and E<sub>a</sub>(reverse) = 30 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. A catalyst lowers BOTH activation energies by the same amount, 25 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. Explain what happens to (a) the forward and reverse rate constants, (b) the equilibrium constant K, and (c) the overall enthalpy change ΔH of the reaction.
options: (a) Both increase; (b) K stays unchanged; (c) ΔH decreases by 25 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, matching the drop applied to each activation energy

(a) Both k(forward) and k(reverse) increase, by exactly the SAME numerical VALUE of k (not just the same drop in Ea), since a shared drop in activation energy of 25 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> produces an identical final rate constant for both directions; (b) K stays unchanged; (c) ΔH stays unchanged
(a) Only k(forward) increases, since the catalyst is assumed to selectively target the forward pathway; (b) K increases; (c) ΔH decreases

(a) Both k(forward) and k(reverse) increase (by different absolute activation energies, 55 and 5 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> respectively after the drop, so their NEW values differ, but the amount by which each was LOWERED is identical); (b) K = k(forward)/k(reverse) stays unchanged, since the difference E<sub>a</sub>(reverse) − E<sub>a</sub>(forward), which is what actually governs ΔH, is unaffected by subtracting the same amount from both; (c) ΔH remains unchanged, since ΔH = E<sub>a</sub>(forward) − E<sub>a</sub>(reverse), and both terms shift down by the identical amount, leaving their DIFFERENCE the same
questions.explanation: (a) Both E<sub>a</sub>(forward) and E<sub>a</sub>(reverse) drop by the same 25 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, giving new values of 55 and 5 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> respectively; since these starting values were different, the resulting new rate constants are also different from each other (though both are larger than before). (b) K = k(forward)/k(reverse) is governed by the DIFFERENCE E<sub>a</sub>(reverse) − E<sub>a</sub>(forward), which stays at 30−80 = −50 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> both before and after catalysis, so K is unchanged. (c) ΔH = E<sub>a</sub>(forward) − E<sub>a</sub>(reverse) for an elementary step is likewise unaffected, since both terms shift by the same amount and their difference is preserved — confirming a catalyst never alters reaction thermodynamics, only kinetics.
questions.hint: Track the DIFFERENCE between forward and reverse activation energies (which determines both K and ΔH) separately from their individual VALUES (which determine the actual rate constants).
distractor_logic: Wrongly assumes ΔH changes; since ΔH = E<sub>a</sub>(forward) − E<sub>a</sub>(reverse) and BOTH terms are reduced by the identical 25 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, their difference (ΔH) is completely unaffected — a catalyst never changes the reaction's overall thermodynamics, only its kinetic pathway.

Correctly identifies that K and ΔH stay unchanged, but wrongly assumes the two (originally very different) rate constants end up numerically EQUAL just because the same 25 kJ/mol was subtracted from each Ea; since the two original Ea values (80 and 30) are different, their post-catalyst values (55 and 5) remain different from each other, and so do the resulting rate constants — it's the AMOUNT of the Ea reduction that's shared, not the final k values.

Wrongly assumes a catalyst can selectively speed up only one direction; by mechanism, any pathway the catalyst opens is shared by both directions, so both forward and reverse rate constants increase together, and (since their ratio K depends only on the Ea DIFFERENCE, unaffected here) K itself does not change.

questions.topic: Effect of Catalyst on Reaction Rate
questions.question: A reaction is second order overall (first order in each of two reactants). A catalyst lowers its activation energy by 20 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> at 310 K, with A unchanged. (a) By what factor does the rate constant increase? (b) Does the reaction's ORDER change as a result of adding the catalyst (R = 8.314 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)?
options: (a) Factor ≈ 49.4; (b) No — a catalyst changes the numerical value of the rate constant (and hence the rate at given concentrations) by providing a lower-Ea pathway, but the empirical order (how rate depends on each reactant's concentration) is a separate property of the rate law and is not automatically changed just because a catalyst is present

(a) Factor ≈ 49.4; (b) Yes — a catalyst that lowers activation energy always also increases the order of a reaction, since the more accessible pathway inherently allows more reactant species to participate at once
(a) Factor ≈ 49.4; (b) The order cannot be determined at all once a catalyst is introduced, since catalysis fundamentally invalidates the original rate law
(a) Factor ≈ 1.06 (mistakenly using kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> directly in the exponent instead of converting to J mol<sup>−1</sup>); (b) No, for the correct reason given
questions.explanation: (a) k(after)/k(before) = e<sup>20000/(8.314×310)</sup> ≈ e<sup>7.76</sup> ≈ 49.4. (b) The order of a reaction depends on its mechanism (specifically the rate-determining step), not directly on the numerical value of the activation energy. If the catalyst provides a genuinely different mechanistic pathway, the order COULD change, but simply lowering Ea via an unspecified catalytic route does not, by itself, guarantee any particular change in the observed order — this would need to be determined experimentally for the specific catalyzed pathway.
questions.hint: Separate the numerical rate-constant effect (predictable from the Arrhenius equation given the Ea change) from the mechanistic question of order (which depends on the specific pathway and needs its own experimental determination).
distractor_logic: Wrongly assumes a lower activation energy necessarily changes the rate law's order; in reality, whether the order changes depends on whether the catalyst introduces a genuinely different mechanism with a different rate-determining step, not simply on the fact that Ea has decreased — many catalyzed reactions retain the same order as their uncatalyzed counterpart.

Wrongly claims the original rate law becomes entirely invalid; a catalyzed reaction still has a well-defined (possibly identical, possibly different) rate law that can be experimentally re-determined — catalysis doesn't make kinetics analysis impossible, it just potentially changes the specific mechanism and hence possibly the specific order.
Fails to convert kJ to J before dividing by RT, producing an exponent far too small and hence a rate factor much closer to 1 than the true value.

questions.topic: Effect of Catalyst on Reaction Rate
questions.question: An uncatalyzed first-order reaction has k = 1.0×10<sup>−5</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> at 300 K and t½ accordingly. A catalyst is introduced that increases k by a factor of 500 at the same temperature. (a) Find the new half-life. (b) If the uncatalyzed E<sub>a</sub> was 100 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, estimate the catalyzed E<sub>a</sub> assuming A is unchanged (R = 8.314 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>).
options: (a) New t½ = old t½/500 is impossible to compute without knowing the old t½ numerically first (a false claim; it is directly computable) — treat as undefined; (b) new E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 84.4 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
(a) New t½ ≈ 1.39×10<sup>3</sup> s (about 23.1 min), 500× shorter than the uncatalyzed t½; (b) new E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 84.4 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (a drop of about 15.6 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>)

(a) New t½ ≈ 1.39×10<sup>3</sup> s; (b) new E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 115.6 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (mistakenly ADDING the calculated change instead of subtracting it, since increasing k must come from DECREASING Ea, not increasing it)
(a) New t½ ≈ 3.47×10<sup>4</sup> s (dividing by 500 incorrectly using k rather than the half-life relationship, introducing an extra factor of 25); (b) new E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 84.4 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: (a) Since t½=0.693/k for first order, and the catalyzed k is 500× the original (5.0×10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>), the new t½ = 0.693/(5.0×10<sup>−3</sup>) ≈ 1.39×10<sup>3</sup> s ≈ 23.1 min, exactly 1/500 of the original half-life. (b) Using k(after)/k(before)=500=e<sup>[Ea(before)−Ea(after)]/RT</sup>, solving gives E<sub>a</sub>(before)−E<sub>a</sub>(after) = RT×ln(500) ≈ 8.314×300×6.215 ≈ 15,502 J mol<sup>−1</sup> ≈ 15.5 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, so new E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 100−15.5 ≈ 84.5 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: For first order, t½ and k are simply inversely proportional; for the Ea change, remember that a k INCREASE always corresponds to an Ea DECREASE.
distractor_logic: Wrongly claims the calculation cannot proceed; since t½=0.693/k for a first-order reaction, and k is quintupled by a factor of 500, t½ simply scales by 1/500 of the original value, fully computable as 0.693/(5.0×10<sup>−3</sup>).

Gets the direction backwards; since a FASTER reaction (larger k) requires a LOWER activation energy (via the Arrhenius equation's negative exponent), the catalyzed Ea must be smaller than 100, not larger.

Makes an arithmetic slip introducing an extraneous factor of 25 rather than correctly recognizing that for a first-order reaction, t½ is simply inversely proportional to k, so a 500-fold increase in k gives exactly a 500-fold decrease in t½, not a 20-fold decrease.

questions.topic: Collision Theory of Chemical Reactions
questions.question: According to collision theory, for a chemical reaction to occur between two colliding molecules, the collision must satisfy which two conditions?
options: The colliding molecules must have combined kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, AND they must collide with the correct (favorable) orientation
The colliding molecules must have low kinetic energy, since high-energy collisions cause molecules to simply bounce apart unreacted
The colliding molecules must simply come into contact; any collision, regardless of energy or orientation, leads to a reaction
The colliding molecules must be of the same chemical substance, since collision theory only applies to reactions between identical molecules
questions.explanation: Collision theory holds that only 'effective' collisions lead to reaction: those where the colliding particles have at least the activation energy AND collide with a geometry that allows the necessary bonds to break and form. Collisions lacking either sufficient energy or proper orientation simply result in the molecules bouncing apart unchanged.
questions.hint: Remember both conditions are necessary together: enough energy AND the right orientation — missing either one means no reaction.
distractor_logic: Has the energy requirement backwards; molecules need SUFFICIENT (high enough) energy, at least equal to the activation energy, to react — low-energy collisions are the ones that simply bounce apart without reacting.

Wrongly assumes every collision is reactive; in reality, only a small fraction of all collisions have both enough energy and the right orientation, which is exactly why reactions proceed at finite, often slow, rates rather than instantaneously.
Incorrectly restricts collision theory to reactions between identical molecules; the theory applies generally to collisions between any two reacting species, whether the same or different substances.

questions.topic: Collision Theory of Chemical Reactions
questions.question: In collision theory, the 'steric factor' (or probability factor), usually given the symbol P, accounts for:
options: the fraction of collisions in which the molecules are oriented correctly (in the right geometric arrangement) for a reaction to occur
the fraction of molecules that have enough kinetic energy to react, regardless of orientation
the total number of collisions occurring per second between all reacting molecules
the temperature dependence of the rate constant
questions.explanation: The full collision-theory rate expression is often written as rate = PZe<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>, where Z is the collision frequency, the exponential term is the energy-sufficient fraction, and P (the steric factor) corrects for the fact that even energetic collisions often fail to react simply because the molecules are not oriented correctly relative to each other at the moment of impact.
questions.hint: P specifically captures the GEOMETRIC/orientation requirement, separate from both collision frequency (Z) and the energy requirement (the exponential term).
distractor_logic: Describes the separate exponential (Boltzmann) energy factor e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup> instead, which accounts for energy sufficiency, not orientation; P specifically addresses geometric arrangement.

Describes the collision frequency factor Z instead, which is a distinct quantity representing how often collisions occur in total, independent of whether any particular collision is correctly oriented.

Confuses P with the exponential term, which is what actually carries the temperature dependence in the Arrhenius/collision-theory expression; P itself is typically treated as roughly independent of temperature.

questions.topic: Collision Theory of Chemical Reactions
questions.question: At T = 350 K, calculate the fraction of molecular collisions that possess kinetic energy equal to or greater than an activation energy of 70.0 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (R = 8.314 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>).
options: f ≈ 0.20 (mistakenly using Ea directly in kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> as the exponent without converting to J mol<sup>−1</sup> or dividing correctly by RT)
f ≈ 3.57×10<sup>−11</sup>
f ≈ 3.57×10<sup>−11</sup> kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (correct numeric value but incorrectly attaching energy units to what should be a dimensionless fraction)
f ≈ 4.05×10<sup>12</sup> (sign error, computing e<sup>+Ea/RT</sup> instead of e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>, which would make the fraction unphysically greater than expected and grow rather than shrink with Ea)
questions.explanation: f = e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup> = e<sup>−70000/(8.314×350)</sup> ≈ 3.57×10<sup>−11</sup>. This tiny, dimensionless fraction shows that even at 350 K, only a very small proportion of collisions possess enough energy to overcome a 70 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> barrier.
questions.hint: This is simply the Boltzmann/energy factor from the Arrhenius equation, evaluated as a pure number (no units) using Ea in J mol−1 and R in J K−1 mol−1.
distractor_logic: Fails to properly convert and divide Ea (in J mol<sup>−1</sup>) by RT before exponentiating, producing a value far too large to be a physically sensible energy-sufficient fraction for a typical Ea.
Gets the correct number but incorrectly assigns it energy units; f is a pure (dimensionless) fraction/probability, with no units at all.
Uses the wrong sign in the exponent; the Boltzmann/energy-sufficient fraction always uses a NEGATIVE exponent (since higher energy requirements make the fraction smaller, not larger).

questions.topic: Collision Theory of Chemical Reactions
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes how collision frequency (Z) and the energy-sufficient fraction each depend on temperature, according to collision theory?
options: Collision frequency Z increases exponentially with temperature, while the energy-sufficient fraction increases only modestly
Both collision frequency and the energy-sufficient fraction are completely independent of temperature; only the steric factor P depends on T
Collision frequency Z increases only modestly with temperature (roughly proportional to √T), while the energy-sufficient fraction increases much more steeply (exponentially) with temperature
Collision frequency Z decreases with increasing temperature, since faster-moving molecules spend less time near each other during any given encounter
questions.explanation: Collision frequency Z depends on average molecular speed, which (from the kinetic theory of gases) scales roughly as the square root of temperature — a relatively gentle increase. The energy-sufficient fraction, however, depends exponentially on T through the Boltzmann factor e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>, which can change dramatically even for modest temperature changes. This is why the overall temperature sensitivity of reaction rate is dominated by the exponential energy term, not by collision frequency.
questions.hint: Collision frequency's T-dependence (√T, gentle) and the energy-sufficient fraction's T-dependence (exponential, steep) are very different in magnitude — this difference explains why rate is so sensitive to temperature overall.
distractor_logic: Swaps the two dependences; it is the ENERGY-SUFFICIENT FRACTION (via the exponential Boltzmann term) that rises steeply with T, while collision frequency itself rises only modestly (roughly as √T from kinetic theory of gases).

Incorrectly claims neither depends on T at all; both collision frequency and (especially) the energy-sufficient fraction genuinely change with temperature, which is precisely why reaction rate is so temperature-sensitive; the steric factor P is typically the one usually treated as roughly T-independent.
Confuses collision frequency with a completely different, unrelated effect; collision frequency in fact slightly INCREASES with temperature (since average molecular speed increases), not decreases.

questions.topic: Collision Theory of Chemical Reactions
questions.question: For an elementary bimolecular reaction with steric factor P = 0.20, collision frequency factor Z = 5.0×10<sup>10</sup> L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, and E<sub>a</sub> = 48.0 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> at T = 310 K, calculate the rate constant k using collision theory, and comment on why the experimentally observed rate constant for many real reactions is often somewhat LOWER than what the simple collision-frequency term Z alone would predict, even after accounting for the energy factor (R = 8.314 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>).
options: k ≈ 408 L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (forgetting to include the steric factor P, using only Z×e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>)

k ≈ 81.6 L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; the steric factor P (here only 0.20, i.e. only 1 in 5 sufficiently energetic collisions is also correctly oriented) is precisely why real rate constants often fall well below the naive Z×e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup> estimate that ignores orientation requirements entirely

k ≈ 81.6 L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; but claims the discrepancy between Z alone and the true rate constant is due ENTIRELY to intermolecular attractive forces, with no role for molecular orientation at all
k ≈ 4.08×10<sup>10</sup> L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (forgetting to include the exponential energy term, using only P×Z)
questions.explanation: k = P×Z×e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup> = 0.20×(5.0×10<sup>10</sup>)×e<sup>−48000/(8.314×310)</sup> ≈ 81.6 L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. Without the steric factor (i.e. using only Z×e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>), the predicted rate constant would be five times larger (≈408). This gap is exactly why real reactions often show measured rate constants noticeably below the simple collision-frequency-times-energy-factor prediction: many energetically sufficient collisions still fail because the molecules are not correctly oriented at the moment of impact, a purely geometric requirement captured only by including P.
questions.hint: Comparing k WITH and WITHOUT the steric factor P shows directly how much of the gap between the naive collision-frequency estimate and the true rate constant is explained by orientation requirements alone.
distractor_logic: Omits the steric factor P, effectively assuming every sufficiently energetic collision is also perfectly oriented to react, which overstates the true rate constant by a factor of 1/P = 5.

Reaches the right numeric answer but gives an incorrect physical explanation; while intermolecular forces can play a role in some cases, the standard and primary reason collision theory's naive Z-based estimate overstates real rate constants is the neglected orientation (steric) requirement, exactly the role played by the factor P.

Omits the exponential energy-sufficient factor entirely, leaving only the collision-frequency-times-orientation product, which vastly overstates the rate constant by ignoring how rarely collisions have sufficient energy.

questions.topic: Collision Theory of Chemical Reactions
questions.question: For an elementary reaction, the Arrhenius pre-exponential factor is found to be A = 1.0×10<sup>10</sup> L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, while the purely geometric collision frequency factor (ignoring orientation) is separately calculated as Z = 2.0×10<sup>11</sup> L mol<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. (a) What does this imply about the steric factor P? (b) A reaction is also confirmed, from concentration-time data, to be second order overall. Is this order consistent with collision theory's PZe<sup>−Ea/RT</sup> model as written?
options: (a) P ≈ Z/A = 20 (mistakenly inverting the ratio, implying an impossible steric factor greater than 1, since a probability factor cannot exceed 1)
(a) P ≈ A/Z = 0.05, correctly; (b) No — collision theory in this simple form applies only to first-order reactions, since only one molecule's energy can be considered at a time

(a) Since A = PZ in the collision-theory framework, P ≈ A/Z = 0.05, meaning only about 1 in 20 sufficiently energetic collisions is favorably oriented; (b) Yes — the simple PZe<sup>−Ea/RT</sup> model is specifically built for elementary bimolecular collisions (rate depending on the product of two reactant concentrations, i.e. overall second order), so a genuinely elementary, second-order reaction is exactly the case this model is designed to describe

(a) P ≈ A/Z = 0.05, correctly; (b) No — a second-order rate law can never correspond to a genuinely elementary bimolecular collision, since order and molecularity are always unrelated concepts by definition
questions.explanation: (a) In collision theory, A (the empirically fitted Arrhenius pre-exponential factor) is identified with PZ (steric factor times theoretical collision frequency), so P = A/Z = (1.0×10<sup>10</sup>)/(2.0×10<sup>11</sup>) = 0.05, meaning only 5% of sufficiently energetic collisions are also correctly oriented. (b) The simple collision-theory expression rate=PZe<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>[A][B] is built specifically for elementary bimolecular reactions, whose rate law is naturally second order overall (first order in each of two colliding species) — so a confirmed second-order, elementary reaction is exactly the situation this model was designed to describe, with order and molecularity coinciding as expected for an elementary step.
questions.hint: A=PZ lets you extract the steric factor from comparing the empirical Arrhenius A to the theoretical collision frequency Z; and the PZe^(−Ea/RT) model itself presumes an elementary bimolecular (hence second-order) step.
distractor_logic: Inverts the defining relationship A=PZ, producing a steric factor greater than 1, which is physically impossible since P represents a fraction (at most 1, i.e. every correctly-energetic collision also correctly oriented) of an already-defined maximum collision frequency.

Wrongly claims collision theory in this simple form is restricted to first-order reactions; in fact, the PZe^(−Ea/RT) framework, with its single collision-frequency term between two species, is specifically built around BIMOLECULAR (and hence naturally second-order, when elementary) collisions.

Wrongly claims order and molecularity are ALWAYS unrelated; they coincide precisely for elementary reactions, and a genuinely elementary bimolecular step (which the collision-theory PZe^(−Ea/RT) model directly describes) is naturally second order overall, making this order fully consistent with, not contradictory to, the model.

Molecularity vs Order of Reaction

questions.topic: Collision Theory of Chemical Reactions
questions.question: At T₁ = 290 K, the fraction of collisions with energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub> = 58.0 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> is calculated to be about 3.57×10<sup>−11</sup>. At T₂ = 330 K, it rises to about 6.59×10<sup>−10</sup>, an 18.5-fold increase. Meanwhile, the collision frequency Z itself (which scales roughly as √T) increases by only about a factor of 1.07 over the same temperature range. Use both these numbers to estimate the overall factor by which the rate constant increases from T₁ to T₂, and use this to explain why the simple Arrhenius two-temperature formula alone (which assumes A, including its embedded Z, is constant with T) is usually still a good approximation.
options: Overall rate-constant factor ≈ 18.5 × 1.07 ≈ 19.8, dominated almost entirely by the exponential energy-sufficient factor (18.5×) rather than the collision-frequency factor (1.07×, barely more than a rounding correction); this is exactly why treating A as roughly constant with T in the simple Arrhenius equation introduces only a small error, since the exponential term overwhelmingly dominates the overall temperature dependence

Overall rate-constant factor ≈ 18.5 alone; this shows the T-dependence of collision frequency is not just small but completely and always exactly zero in every case, meaning A should never be treated as even approximately temperature-dependent under any circumstances
Overall rate-constant factor ≈ 18.5 + 1.07 ≈ 19.6 (incorrectly ADDING the two factors instead of multiplying them, since they represent independently multiplicative contributions to the overall rate)

Overall rate-constant factor ≈ 1.07 alone, since only the collision-frequency term Z is treated as a 'real' physical quantity in collision theory, with the exponential term regarded as a purely mathematical correction with no independent physical significance
questions.explanation: Since rate constant ∝ Z×(energy-sufficient fraction), the overall multiplicative increase from T₁ to T₂ is approximately 18.5×1.07 ≈ 19.8. Because the collision-frequency factor's contribution (1.07×, i.e. only about a 7% increase) is so small compared to the exponential energy term's contribution (18.5×), treating A as roughly constant with temperature in the simple Arrhenius equation introduces only a small error in practice — the vast majority of the observed temperature sensitivity of rate genuinely comes from the exponential Boltzmann factor, not from collision frequency.
questions.hint: The two contributions to temperature sensitivity multiply together, but since one (collision frequency) is so much smaller than the other (the exponential energy term), approximating it as constant barely affects the overall result.
distractor_logic: Overstates the case; while the collision-frequency factor's T-dependence (roughly √T) is genuinely small compared to the exponential term over most practical ranges, it is not EXACTLY zero — treating A as constant is a good APPROXIMATION for many purposes, not an exact truth in all circumstances.

Combines the two multiplicative factors using addition instead of multiplication; since rate constant is proportional to the PRODUCT of the collision-frequency term and the energy-sufficient fraction, their combined effect on k is likewise multiplicative (18.5×1.07), not additive.

Wrongly dismisses the exponential (energy-sufficient) term as merely a 'mathematical correction'; it is every bit as physically real as the collision-frequency term, representing the genuine physical fact that only sufficiently energetic collisions can react, and in practice it is the DOMINANT physical contributor to temperature sensitivity, not a secondary one.
